who: Low vision users who miss targets
Anyone who taps the wrong thing
takeaways: For single-pointer actions, pressing down does not complete the action. It completes on release.
Then people can slide off the target before letting go to cancel. Or, if it fires, they can undo it.
Press-and-hold that shows something, like a preview, is fine if letting go hides it again.
Exception: acting on press is essential, such as playing a note on a piano app. This is mostly built by developers; you decide which actions are risky and how undo works.
failures: Buttons that fire the moment a finger touches them
A delete that happens on press with no undo
Drag and drop that cannot be cancelled once picked up
check: In the build, press a button, slide off it and release. Did anything happen?
List the destructive actions and confirm each has undo or a way to cancel.
Check that drag and drop cancels when dropped outside a valid target.

quiz.question: Engineers want a “Delete” button to fire on touch-down so it feels faster. What do you recommend?
options: Fire on press. Speed matters most
Fire on release, and cancel if the finger slides off
Fire on press, with a confirmation dialog every time
quiz.why: Release is the moment people can still change their mind. Acting on press removes that chance, and a dialog on every delete adds friction for everyone.

spec: State that actions complete on release, not on press.
Design the pressed state, so people see the action is about to happen.
For risky actions, specify the undo, such as a toast with an Undo button.
review: What happens if someone touches this by mistake?
Is there any reason this must fire on press?
tradeoff: Acting on press can feel snappier in games and music apps. Outside those cases, a clear pressed state gives the same feeling of speed while keeping the chance to back out.
system: Base button and list-item components fire on release, and destructive actions use a standard undo toast.
pitch: Everyone has tapped the wrong thing. Firing on release means a slip costs nothing.
